description: We built a web application that combines historical heat-source records from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites, filters out false detections such as the Sabancaya volcano, which appears as a permanent fire and converts the data into a calendar showing which districts in the region are burning and during which weeks of the year.
summary:
Peru has a national wildfire plan, and it does name priority districts. But of the 177 districts that hold eighty percent of the country's detected burning, only 31 are on that list. Institutions plan prevention without a district-level answer to the simplest question: when does my district actually burn?
The answer is locked inside two satellite records that cannot be added together. MODIS has watched since November 2000 at 1 km; VIIRS since January 2012 at 375 m. VIIRS sees smaller fires, so counting both as one invents a rise that never happened, and Terra and Aqua have drifted hours from their original overpass times, so even MODIS cannot be compared against itself across 26 years.
ChillSpace harmonizes them. A chained splice brings every detection to a common MODIS-equivalent scale, corrected for coverage, with a Poisson uncertainty interval on every value and a state label on every figure. The result is a burn calendar for all 1,849 districts of Peru, from November 2000 to the present month, with the months and the few square kilometres where each district's burning concentrates.
The tool runs for the whole country and is validated in Arequipa.
details:
What exactly does it do?

ChillSpace is a seasonal prevention planner built on a harmonized satellite record. Specifically:

  • Puts MODIS and VIIRS hot spots on one comparable scale across 26 years (November 2000 to the present month), without ever adding the two sensors together.
  • Shows a burn calendar for any of Peru's 1,849 districts, 25 departments or the whole country: one cell per month, measured against that month's own historical median.
  • Names, district by district, the months that hold half of its burning. In 706 of the 1,416 ranked districts half the country two months are enough; the national median is three.
  • Gives the area in square kilometres where half of a district's events concentrate, so a campaign knows not only when but where. In Arequipa that median is 14 km².
  • Ranks districts for seasonal prevention and generates a printable campaign sheet per district.
  • Flags months whose activity departs from that place's own history, separating a real anomaly from a change in which satellite was watching.
  • Answers questions in plain words through an assistant that reads the same numbers the screens show, and writes the campaign sheet on request.
  • Shows every detection on a 3D terrain map, one month at a time.

Every figure carries a state label observed, harmonized, estimated and links to the methodology page that explains how it was computed.

How does it work?

1. Ingest. Seven FIRMS files are concatenated: the historical archives and the near-real-time feeds for each sensor family. Archive and NRT do not overlap, so no de-duplication across sets is needed. Detections are matched against INEI district boundaries.

2. Quality filtering. MODIS keeps type = 0(vegetation) with confidence 30 or above; VIIRS keeps type = 0 at nominal or high confidence. Volcanoes, gas flares and industrial heat (types 1, 2 and 3) are excluded, along with pixels affected by sensor faults. Confidence is not comparable between families MODIS reports 0–100, VIIRS reports low/nominal/high so it is normalised to a three-level scale. A catalogue of 65 permanent heat sources is excluded outright.

3. Harmonization by chained splice. This is the core of the work, and the reason we do not anchor to MODIS. Terra's overpass has drifted from 15.87 h in 2000 to 13.77 h in 2026, and Aqua's from 18.48 h in 2002 to 20.60 h in 2026: late-period MODIS detects less fire without there being less fire, so it cannot serve as the yardstick. Instead the series is spliced in segments, each factor estimated in a window where both sensors were stable:

  • November 2000 to January 2012: MODIS alone.
  • January 2012 to April 2018: S-NPP, scaled by the first factor.
  • April 2018 to today: NOAA-20, scaled by the first and second factors.

A coverage correction accounts for the months a sensor was not delivering. Missing data is carried as null, never as zero.

4. Uncertainty. A detection count is a counting process, so its statistical uncertainty has a closed form. Every harmonized value carries a 95% Poisson interval by Byar's approximation — chosen over the normal approximation because roughly 95% of district-month cells are zero or near-zero, where the normal approximation fails. The interval captures counting noise; it does not include the uncertainty of the inter-sensor calibration, and we say so on the page.

5. Events and regimes. A Random Forest classifier separates vegetation burning from other heat. DBSCAN groups detections into events, so a single fire seen by several pixels is counted once. Districts are grouped into burn regimes by the shape of their monthly profile, ignoring geography.

6. Validation. The harmonized series is checked against NASA's MCD64A1 burned-area product across eight districts: concordance ratios run from 5.3× to 14.1×, all significant at p < 0.05. FRP across the two families follows a power law with c = 1.343 and k = −0.098 over 39,084 matched pairs.

7. Delivery. The pipeline runs offline and freezes its output to JSON. The web application reads those files it never recomputes. One source of truth, and a method version stamped on every figure.

What benefits does it have?

Institutional. A municipality, a regional government, a fire brigade or SERFOR can put prevention on a calendar instead of improvising it. The tool names the two or three months that hold half of a district's burning and the few square kilometres where it concentrates, which is what a firebreak, a patrol rota or an awareness campaign actually needs. It also shows which of the districts that burn most are absent from the national plan.

Social. Prevention aimed at the right month and the right place costs less and reaches further than suppression. Andean districts with small populations and thin budgets gain the same evidence base that a large city has.

Scientific. The harmonized record is reusable beyond this app. Separating a genuine change in fire activity from a change in which satellite was watching is a problem every long FIRMS time series has, and the chained splice with its coverage correction is our answer to it, published with its uncertainty and its limits rather than as a single confident number.

Transparency as a feature. Every figure carries a state label and links to the method that produced it, so a technician can check our arithmetic instead of trusting it.

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, to put ChillSpace in front of the institutions that plan prevention in Arequipa and to have one of them use it to set the months and the zones of a real campaign. That is the validation that matters: not a better chart, a decision taken earlier than it would have been.

In the medium term, to close the gap the data already shows: the 146 districts that hold eighty percent of the country's detected burning and are not in the Plan Multisectorial. Each needs its own calendar, and each now has one.

In the long term, the harmonization is not specific to Peru. Any country with a long FIRMS record faces the same break in 2012 and the same orbital drift. The method, the uncertainty treatment and the refusal to add sensors together travel; only the boundaries change.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages. TypeScript, Python, SQL.

Data pipeline (Python). Python, for the harmonization, the Random Forest classifier, the DBSCAN event grouping and the matching of detections to INEI district boundaries. [Confirm the exact libraries with whoever ran the pipeline: it lives outside the web repository.] Output frozen to compact JSON (base-36 encoded) so the web app loads 26 years of 1,849 districts without a backend.

Frontend. React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS 4, Zustand for UI state, Zod for runtime contract validation, i18next for Spanish and English, Recharts for charts, a hand-built SVG heatmap for the burn calendar, Motion and GSAP for transitions.

Geospatial and 3D. MapLibre GL 6.16 with terrain for the 3D map, three.js for the opening satellite scene (real orbital altitudes and inclinations; satellite positions are illustrative and labelled as such).

Reports. @react-pdf/renderer for the printable campaign sheet.

Assistant. A Supabase Edge Function (Deno) in front of an OpenAI-compatible model endpoint, with a shared daily quota, per-visitor rate limits and an allowed-origin check. The assistant reads the same frozen data the screens read, through a shared facts layer, so it cannot state a number the page does not show.

Infrastructure. Vercel for hosting and deployment, Supabase for the assistant function and its usage table, GitHub for source control.

Testing and quality. Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for browser walkthroughs, oxlint, axe-core for accessibility, TypeScript in strict mode.

Hardware. Development laptops: ChillSpace is built entirely on satellite records and public boundary data.

How is your project creative? What factors did your team consider?

The creative decision was subtractive. The obvious build is to add MODIS and VIIRS together and show one rising line: it looks impressive and it is wrong, because the rise is the second satellite arriving. We refused the single number and built the harmonization instead, then made the uncertainty visible rather than hiding it behind a clean figure. A tool that says "between 11 and 30" is harder to design than one that says "19", and it is the only honest answer when the median district-month is near zero.

The calendar as the interface. Fire data is usually shown as a map of dots. But a prevention officer does not ask where are the dots, they ask which month do I prepare for. So the primary screen is a calendar 26 years down, 12 months across and the map is the second question, not the first.
